title: Paul Graham on startups: do things that don't scale, launch early, pick determined founders
summary: In a Startup School conversation with Geoff Ralston, Paul Graham recounts how ViaWeb started and distills lessons on co-founders, manual early work, launching a quantum of utility fast, and why determination beats smarts. He also covers competitors, pricing, raising too much money, and user interviews.

principles.text: Do things that don't scale early: handmade, manual work for first customers teaches you the most.
principles.quote: what do things that don't scale means is do those things early on anyway because you know if you don't do them you'll never be big and you've got nothing to lose and also you learn a lot from it

principles.text: A constant growth rate compounds, so early on just keep manually getting the next customer.
principles.quote: as long as your growth rate is good it doesn't matter how small the number is because a grow a constant growth rate means exponential growth and that means the base number will soon take care of itself

principles.text: Launch as soon as one person would be glad you did; launching late is a risk too.
principles.quote: launch as soon as you have a quantum of utility which means as soon as you're there's one person in the world who is glad that you launched

principles.text: Determination matters far more than smarts for founders.
principles.quote: it's not that important to be smart um it's much much more important to be determined

principles.text: Competitors rarely kill startups; poor execution does. Just run your own race.
principles.quote: what makes companies fail most of the time is poor execution by the founders

principles.text: Founders' typical mistake is avoiding users and shipping too slowly; find someone with a problem and fix it.
principles.quote: you'd be way better off finding someone anyone who has a problem that they will pay you to fix and fixing it and then seeing if you can find more people like that
